title: I love speed. We all love speed. But what happens when the speed is slowing you down?
gist: The right way to compare LLMs for agentic work is neither benchmark accuracy nor tokens per second but expected time to a validated correct result — Time per Attempt divided by Probability of Success per Attempt — which can make a sparse MoE like Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (3B active params) beat the stronger dense Qwen3.8-27B when the environment supplies cheap objective feedback, and can make the slower Q5_K_M quantization finish faster than Q4_K_M by avoiding correction loops. The piece proposes a concrete replacement benchmark, Persistent Challenge Completion, that fixes wall-clock budget instead of retry count and scores the area under the completion curve plus Recovery Quality.

insights.claim: For autonomous agents, coding agents, research systems and tool-using assistants, neither 'which model is smarter' nor 'which model is faster' identifies the model that will do the most useful work; the operative question is which model reaches a correct result fastest.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Model-selection decisions and vendor comparisons built on leaderboard scores or tokens-per-second are optimizing the wrong objective for agentic deployments.
insights.quote: The optimal model is therefore not necessarily the smartest model or the fastest model.
insights.locator: When comparing large language models

insights.claim: A usable first-order metric for interactive agents is Expected Time to Success = Time per Attempt divided by Probability of Success per Attempt.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Gives a one-line formula for converting latency and accuracy into a single comparable cost number when choosing between models or quantizations.
insights.quote: Expected Time to Success = Time per Attempt / Probability of Success per Attempt
insights.locator: From Intelligence to Intelligence per Second

insights.claim: Applying the formula, a model taking 60 seconds at 90% success yields 66.7 seconds expected time to success while a model taking 20 seconds at only 60% success yields 33.3 seconds — the far less reliable model finishes roughly twice as fast.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Quantifies how much accuracy a 3x speed advantage can buy, justifying deployment of cheaper small models where verification is automatic.
insights.locator: From Intelligence to Intelligence per Second

insights.claim: The useful unit of computation for agents is not accuracy per generation but progress toward a validated solution per second, because a failed attempt leaves behind information the agent retains.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Reframes inference spend as purchasing progress rather than tokens, which is how agent products should be priced and measured.
insights.quote: progress toward a validated solution per second
insights.locator: From Intelligence to Intelligence per Second

insights.claim: Because agent attempts are not independent — a coding agent inspects a traceback, modifies three lines and reruns the test rather than restarting blind — real-world dependence between attempts strengthens rather than weakens the case for speed.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: The naive independent-trials model understates fast models' advantage, so simulated expected-time math is a conservative floor, not an upper bound.
insights.quote: Real agents are more complicated because attempts are not independent. In fact, this often strengthens the argument for speed.
insights.locator: From Intelligence to Intelligence per Second

themes.theme: Dense vs sparse MoE tradeoff in practice

insights.claim: Qwen3.8-27B is a dense 27-billion-parameter model positioned by Qwen for stronger coding, reasoning, professional work and long-horizon agentic execution, with official results of 89.2 on GPQA Diamond, 90.3 on LiveCodeBench v6 and 79.5 on IFBench.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Concrete capability anchor for a 27B dense open model, useful for judging how far open weights trail frontier closed models on reasoning and code.
insights.locator: Intelligence and Speed Are Different Resources

insights.claim: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with roughly 35 billion total parameters but only about 3 billion activated per token, explicitly designed by Qwen for high-throughput inference at relatively low computational cost, scoring 84.2 on GPQA Diamond, 74.6 on LiveCodeBench v6 and 70.2 on IFBench.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: A ~12x ratio of total to active parameters shows how MoE decouples capability storage from per-token compute — the core economics behind cheap high-volume inference.
insights.locator: Intelligence and Speed Are Different Resources

insights.claim: The gap between the two Qwen models is largest on coding (90.3 versus 74.6 on LiveCodeBench v6) and smallest on graduate-level science questions (89.2 versus 84.2 on GPQA Diamond), indicating sparse activation costs more on code generation than on knowledge-style reasoning.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: MoE cost savings are not uniform across workloads — code-heavy agent products pay the steepest quality tax for going sparse.
insights.locator: Intelligence and Speed Are Different Resources

insights.claim: The author explicitly cautions that the two models' benchmark methodologies are not identical enough to constitute a controlled head-to-head experiment, and treats the capability ranking as a reasonable inference rather than a measured fact.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Published vendor benchmark tables are not comparable across model families — a standing caveat when underwriting claimed model leadership.
insights.quote: The benchmark methodologies are not identical enough to claim that these numbers constitute a perfectly controlled head-to-head experiment.
insights.locator: Intelligence and Speed Are Different Resources

insights.claim: In the author's worked example, a dense model needing 60 seconds per attempt at 85% first-attempt success can be beaten by an MoE needing 15 seconds at 65%, because the MoE fits four feedback-informed attempts inside the dense model's single generation.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Justifies deploying cheaper sparse models in verified-feedback environments, shifting inference demand toward high-throughput serving rather than peak-quality serving.
insights.locator: Suppose, purely as an example, the dense model takes 60 seconds

insights.claim: For difficult one-shot questions with no external verification the dense Qwen3.8-27B is preferred, while for an autonomous software-development agent the sparse Qwen3.5-35B-A3B can become much more competitive because the environment itself acts as a critic.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Model choice should be routed by whether the workload has an automatic verifier — a concrete routing rule for multi-model inference stacks.
insights.quote: More attempts do not help if the system does not know the first answer was wrong.
insights.locator: The Qwen3.8 vs. Qwen3.5 MoE Problem

insights.claim: Every task has an intelligence threshold: below it speed is nearly irrelevant because a model that fundamentally cannot solve the problem merely produces ten failures faster, while above it speed becomes extremely important.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Caps the substitution of cheap fast models for capable ones — there is a hard capability floor per task class that no amount of throughput buys around.
insights.quote: Speed can compensate for an elevated error rate; it cannot compensate indefinitely for missing capability.
insights.locator: There is a limit, of course

insights.claim: In llama.cpp reference measurements on one published test model, Q4_K_M raised perplexity by roughly 0.175 over baseline versus roughly 0.057 for Q5_K_M, so the cheaper quantization carries about three times the quantization error.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Puts a measured number on the quality cost of the most popular local-inference quantization, the input needed for any break-even calculation.
insights.locator: Quantization Creates the Same Problem Inside a Single Model

insights.claim: The speed advantage of smaller quantizations is hardware-dependent rather than universal: it materializes on memory-bandwidth-constrained systems where fewer bytes must move per generated token.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Quantization choice is a function of the memory subsystem, so inference-cost models that ignore bandwidth constraints will misprice deployments.
insights.locator: The speed difference is hardware-dependent rather than universal

insights.claim: A worked case shows Q4_K_M at 40 seconds and 72% success ties exactly with Q5_K_M at 50 seconds and 90% success, both at 55.6 seconds expected time, demonstrating that a 20% speed edge is worth about an 18-point success-rate gap here.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Shows how easily headline speed advantages evaporate once reliability is priced in — the same arithmetic applies to cheaper-but-weaker API tiers.
insights.locator: Imagine Q4_K_M completes an average attempt in 40 seconds

insights.claim: A break-even rule for two quantizations of the same model states that the lower-precision option wins when P(Q4)/P(Q5) exceeds T(Q4)/T(Q5), meaning a quant running in 80% of the time can tolerate roughly a 20% relative drop in success probability.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: A directly computable decision rule that replaces folklore like 'Q4_K_M is the best quant' with a per-deployment test.
insights.locator: That gives us a useful break-even rule

insights.claim: In the author's illustration, Q4 needs 45 seconds for an initial patch plus 20 and 25 seconds of correction cycles for 90 seconds total, while Q5's single 55-second patch passes — so measuring generation speed alone picks the wrong winner.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Demonstrates 'faster by being slower' concretely: end-to-end task timing, not tokens per second, is the number to benchmark before procurement.
insights.quote: This is where Q5_K_M can potentially become faster by being slower.
insights.locator: Why Coding Makes Precision More Valuable

insights.claim: Whether Q5 fits entirely in VRAM decides the outcome: if both fit, the real-world speed gap may be small enough that there is little reason not to use the higher-precision quant, but if Q5 forces partial CPU offloading while Q4 stays GPU-resident, the situation reverses dramatically.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: VRAM capacity thresholds create step-function economics in local inference, which is why incremental GPU memory is disproportionately valuable to on-prem AI buyers.
insights.quote: The model does not exist separately from the machine running it.
insights.locator: There Is No Universal "Best Quant"

insights.claim: The best quantization varies by workload: Q4 for casual conversation and high-volume summarization, multiple fast generations for brainstorming, Q5 for coding agents whose reliability gain removes correction loops, and higher precision for mathematical reasoning where no automatic verifier exists.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Workload-by-workload quant routing is an unexploited efficiency lever for anyone running mixed inference fleets.
insights.locator: There Is No Universal "Best Quant"

themes.theme: Cost of failure and error compounding

insights.claim: Failures are not fungible: a syntax error, a wrong variable name or a failed unit test is cheap to correct, an architectural mistake can cost five extra iterations built on a bad assumption, and a silent logic error is worse still because the program runs and the error survives validation.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Error severity, not error rate, drives agent cost — so evaluation must track silent-failure rate, the failure type that both cheap models and quick benchmarks hide.
insights.quote: A silent logic error can be worse still. The program runs, the agent thinks it succeeded, and the error survives validation.
insights.locator: Why Coding Makes Precision More Valuable

insights.claim: Where expensive failure modes dominate, a very small increase in model quality can produce a disproportionately large reduction in total runtime.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Non-linear returns to quality justify paying premium prices for marginal capability in agentic workloads, contradicting commodity-inference pricing logic.
insights.locator: Why Coding Makes Precision More Valuable

insights.claim: A 3% reduction in the probability of making the correct choice at any single step does not produce a 3% worse agent; across a long trajectory of hundreds of decisions it compounds into substantially more failed branches, backtracking, tool calls and repeated generation.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Reliability compounds multiplicatively over agent trajectory length, which is why small benchmark deltas translate into large differences in real agent cost and completion.
insights.quote: Across a long trajectory, it can produce substantially more failed branches, backtracking, tool calls, and repeated generation.
insights.locator: Failure Amplification

insights.claim: Quantization losses that look almost insignificant on conventional language-model benchmarks matter far more inside long-horizon agents because of this compounding, while simultaneously being neutralized by speed when errors are easily observable and recoverable.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Perplexity-style quantization evaluations systematically mislead about agentic deployment risk; the workload's feedback quality decides which effect dominates.
insights.quote: The workload decides which effect dominates.
insights.locator: Failure Amplification

insights.claim: The deciding variable between favoring speed and favoring reliability is the cost of failure, not token generation speed: cheap, obvious, easily corrected failures make speed extraordinarily valuable, while hard-to-detect or cascading failures make reliability more valuable.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Gives a single diagnostic question for any AI deployment decision — how expensive is a wrong answer here — that determines the whole model and hardware stack.
insights.quote: The deciding variable is not token generation speed.
insights.locator: The Fastest Model Is Not Always the Fastest Model

themes.theme: Benchmark gap and the PCC proposal

insights.claim: Current LLM evaluation is fragmented across reasoning accuracy benchmarks, coding benchmarks, tokens-per-second inference tests and perplexity degradation measurements, none of which answers how many tasks a system completes before a clock runs out.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: A structural gap in the evaluation market: whoever operationalizes end-to-end validated-work benchmarking becomes the reference for agent procurement decisions.
insights.locator: The Missing Benchmark: End-to-End Useful Work

insights.claim: The proposed Persistent Challenge Completion benchmark gives a model a difficult, objectively verifiable task and requires it to keep working until it succeeds or a wall-clock budget expires, judging it on recovery rather than on its first answer.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Shifts the fixed resource from retry count to wall-clock time, which is the only construction that lets fast and slow models compete on equal economic terms.
insights.quote: Give the model a difficult, objectively verifiable task and require it to keep going until it succeeds or the time budget expires.
insights.locator: A Proposed Benchmark: Persistent Challenge Completion

insights.claim: The proposed primary metric is Validated Work per Second — successfully completed tasks divided by total wall-clock time — with the most important aggregate being the area under the completion curve, formalized as PCC Score = (1/N) × Σ (B − tᵢ)/B with unsolved tasks scoring zero.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Rewards early completion rather than eventual completion, matching how agent value actually accrues in production throughput terms.
insights.quote: VWS = Number of successfully completed tasks / Total wall-clock time
insights.locator: Primary Metrics

insights.claim: Recovery Quality, defined as the probability of success within budget conditional on the first attempt having failed, is proposed as a second headline metric that separates models suited to interactive environments from those better at one-shot tasks.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Recovery ability is an orthogonal, currently unmeasured axis of model value — models with modest first-attempt accuracy but strong recovery are systematically underrated.
insights.quote: Recovery Quality = P(success within budget | first attempt failed)
insights.locator: The Benchmark's Hardest Requirement

insights.claim: A persistence benchmark must distinguish useful iteration from blind repetition by recording progress signals such as more tests passing, fewer compiler errors or reduced validator distance, and by flagging repeated near-identical actions as a persistence failure rather than a strategy.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Loop detection is the key integrity mechanism separating real agent capability from expensive churn — a direct cost line in production agent deployments.
insights.locator: Measuring Persistence Rather Than Random Repetition

insights.claim: The benchmark is structured in five escalating difficulty tiers — local correction from a clear error message, multi-file implementation, ambiguous debugging requiring hypothesis formation, long-horizon engineering, and adversarial or deceptive validation with misleading symptoms and hidden tests.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: A tiered completion curve reveals the highest complexity a system can reliably finish, which is the practical question for automating real engineering work.
insights.locator: Difficulty Tiers

insights.claim: Fair model comparison requires holding the harness constant — same system prompt, tool definitions, context limits, environment, validator, permissions and time budget — with a separate optimized-system track that permits tuning only if the full configuration is published.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Two-track evaluation acknowledges that agent value is a system property, so published harness configuration becomes as important as the model checkpoint.
insights.quote: the benchmark is ultimately about systems, not isolated model checkpoints
insights.locator: Controlling the Agent Harness

insights.claim: Validators must be hidden or hard to exploit — using hidden tests, randomized inputs, multiple valid solution paths, state checks that a fake response cannot satisfy and validation after the agent terminates — because visible tests encourage agents to hard-code expected outputs.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Reward hacking is the default failure mode of verifiable-task benchmarks, so public agent leaderboards with visible tests should be discounted.
insights.locator: Preventing Benchmark Gaming

insights.claim: Two models with identical first-attempt scores can produce opposite system outcomes: a 50% first-attempt model might reach 90% completion after thirty minutes of persistent interaction by iterating quickly, or stall at 55% if its failures are simply not recoverable.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: First-attempt benchmark scores carry almost no information about deployed agent performance, undermining the leaderboard-driven model procurement now standard in the industry.
insights.quote: The same first-attempt score can therefore produce very different system outcomes.
insights.locator: Why This Benchmark Would Change Model Selection

insights.claim: Under a persistence benchmark, a Q4 model might show lower first-attempt accuracy yet a higher completion rate under a generous time budget while a Q5 model dominates under short budgets by avoiding correction loops, making the crossover point measurable rather than speculative.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Time budget becomes an explicit configuration variable in deployment: latency-sensitive products and batch products should run different quantizations of the same model.
insights.locator: Why This Benchmark Would Change Model Selection

insights.claim: Whether an agent succeeds within a budget is modeled as a function of seven variables — task-solving intelligence, output quality, inference and action speed, environmental feedback quality, recovery ability, cost of failure and available time — with no universal ordering of models under that function.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Formalizes why 'best model' leaderboards are incoherent for agents: rankings invert with task distribution and environment, so buyers must evaluate in their own environment.
insights.quote: P(success by time B) = f(I, Q, S, F, R, C, B)
insights.locator: A More Complete Performance Equation

insights.claim: The properties most worth rewarding in a model are behavioral rather than raw: treating an error message as evidence, abandoning a bad plan instead of repeating it confidently, and verifying its own work rather than stopping at an attractive-looking artifact.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Post-training for failure handling and self-verification is a differentiation axis distinct from scale — a place where smaller labs can beat bigger models on deployed value.
insights.quote: Most importantly, the benchmark would reward models that know how to use failure.
insights.locator: Why This Benchmark Would Change Model Selection

insights.claim: Persistence must not mean endless activity — a strong agent should detect failure, identify the causal evidence, update its hypothesis, choose a materially different corrective action, preserve useful progress, revert harmful changes, allocate time between investigation and implementation, and stop only when success is verified or remaining budget is useless.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: This eight-item list is a practical capability checklist for evaluating any autonomous coding agent product beyond its demo.
insights.locator: The Benchmark's Hardest Requirement

insights.claim: Results should be published as a speed-quality frontier — completion rate at several time budgets, median time to success, first-attempt accuracy, final success after persistence, cost per successful task, token and tool usage, and failure and recovery behavior — because a single leaderboard number hides whether a model is strong-but-slow, weak-but-fast, or prone to unproductive loops.
insights.speaker: Sonny DeSorbo
insights.so_what: Cost per successful task is the metric that maps model choice directly to unit economics, and it is absent from every mainstream leaderboard today.
insights.quote: A single leaderboard number can hide these differences. A completion curve reveals them.
insights.locator: Reporting the Speed-Quality Frontier
